title: Shortcut Bench
description: Two trays that hold the same numbers in different arrangements, a strip that breaks a number up before multiplying it, and a rail where zeros do the work.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

bands.footer: 758 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it, the phase dots and the phase and question counts at the right.

writeup.why: Find out what you are allowed to change about a multiplication without changing its answer, and let the zeros of a round number do the work.
writeup.look: Two trays side by side sharing one set of number cards, an expand and add strip below them and a rail of opening zeros along the foot.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Shortcut Bench' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the arrangements worked against the arrangements standing on the bench, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each tray lands a product and the second fixed at what the bench is holding. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. Two trays stand across the top of the working area, each 500 by 200, the left at 64,202 and the right at 650,202, with a still gap of 86 between them that never holds anything. One set of number cards belongs to both trays: a card is 132 by 96, drawn as a solid plate with its number large, and the same card can stand in either tray. A swap control under a tray reverses the cards in it. Brackets are drawn as two heavy curves that close around any pair in a three card tray, and the bracketed pair is then worked first and held afterwards as one card with its own number on it. A one card and a zero card sit on the bench corner at 1020,158 and can be dropped into either tray at any time, the tray handing the long number straight back for the one and collapsing visibly to nothing for the zero. Both trays work at once and their products land together on a shared ledge under the gap, side by side and level, and under each product its own working is drawn out in full so that the two pieces of working can be read against one another as well as the two answers. The expand and add strip opens beneath the trays, 1086 by 132 at 64,428: it writes the multiplicand as its hundreds, tens and ones with plus signs 28 tall between them, gives each part its own small row and its own product, and adds those rows back, with the whole number worked alongside in a column of its own. The zeros rail runs along the foot, 1086 by 108 at 64,592: the number sits on it with closed places drawn to its right, and multiplying by ten, a hundred or a thousand opens one, two or three of them, the digits sliding left as the places open and every place naming itself as it fills, the opening zeros drawn grey because they are holding places and not counting anything. For a multiple such as sixty or eight hundred the short fact is worked above the rail first and only then are the multiplier's own zeros opened. The pairing bay sits at the right of the rail, 320 by 108, taking three cards and, once the child has chosen, lighting whichever two of them multiply to a round number. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a product or a part of one is asked for, and on the second and fourth phases a choice pad holding the arrangements themselves, so that an order or a pair can be picked with one press instead of typed out. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product standing under the rule is green; a digit carried into the next column is vermilion and is always drawn small and inside a ring set above the column it is joining, never in the margin and never under the rule; a partial product row made by one place of the multiplier is rose; and a zero that is only holding a place open, or a step that is skipped, is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading written above it before it is ever told by a colour, and a carried digit by being small and by sitting in a ring above the column it is going into.
writeup.finish: The card shows one product worked two ways with its answers together, and the number from the zeros rail with its places still open.

phases.win: the first tray hands the number back unchanged and the second collapses to nothing
phases.does: drops each card in turn and reads what came back
phases.goal: a product with one gives the number back and a product with zero gives nothing
phases.says: Take the number once. Now take it no times at all. What came back each time?
phases.check: What is 56,902 x 1, and what is 9,63,201 x 0?
phases.feels: two cards that need no working at all, whatever number happens to be in the tray
phases.hands: On paper write any number you like and multiply it by one, then by zero. Do it again with a number long enough to fill the line, and again with a number only two digits long. Ask whether the length of the number made any difference to either of the two answers.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many times is the number in the tray being taken? Second rung, the phase's: what is left when a number is taken no times at all? Third rung: the tray is cut to a two digit number and the child drops each of the two cards into it in turn. The choice pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: one and zero both look like small quiet numbers that leave things alone, and a child who has just watched one hand a number back expects the next small card to do something of the same kind.
wrong.move: gives the number itself as the answer to the zero, by treating zero the way one had just behaved.
wrong.screen: the tray holding the number is emptied slowly out onto the bench as equal groups, and then the zero card asks for that many groups to be taken: the bench counts out no groups at all and stands bare, with the child's answer left in the slot beside the empty bench and nothing marked.

wrong.why: two odd little cards offered together look like two halves of one rule, and the rule that was just heard was about nothing being left.
wrong.move: answers zero for the product with one as well, because the two cards were dropped into the tray in the same breath.
wrong.screen: the two cards separate and are worked in two rows one above the other, each with a tray of its own: the one row hands the long number back digit for digit with the two readings stood together and matching, and the zero row collapses to nothing. Neither row is cleared while the other runs.

phases.screen: a tray holding one long number, with a one card and a zero card waiting beside it
phases.soWhat: Multiplying by one gives the number back unchanged, and multiplying by zero gives zero.
phases.concept: One leaves it alone and zero flattens it

phases.win: both trays land on the same product and the pairing bay lights the pair that makes a round number
phases.does: works both trays and reads the two products against each other
phases.goal: swapping the cards, or bracketing a different pair, leaves the product alone
phases.says: Swap them over, then work both trays. Did the product move?
phases.check: 512 x 2 comes to 1024. Without multiplying anything, what does 2 x 512 come to, and does its working have to look the same?
phases.feels: the arrangement is a free choice, and the answer does not care which choice was made
phases.hands: Write one multiplication on paper and work it in full. Then write the same two numbers with their positions swapped and work that in full as well. Hold the two answers together, then hold the two pieces of working together, and ask which of the two they would rather have had to write out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which cards are standing in the tray? Second rung, the phase's: what does changing their order do to the product? Third rung: both trays are cut to two small cards each and the child works the two arrangements by hand. The choice pad stays open.

wrong.why: a rule has just been heard, and a rule heard is a reason to stop working; copying across is what a rule of that kind seems to be for.
wrong.move: works only the left tray and copies its answer into the right one, because the cards are the same and the answer is bound to be.
wrong.screen: the right tray works its own arrangement anyway, slowly, every step drawn where the child could have drawn it, and the two products land side by side on the ledge and match. The two pieces of working are then stood one above the other, where they are plainly not the same shape, with the rows of each counted along the margin. The copied answer is left exactly where it was put and nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a bench of loose cards invites everything on it to be rearranged, and the rule that was just given said the arrangement was a free choice.
wrong.move: changes one of the cards as well as the order, because swapping and rewriting feel like the same tidying up.
wrong.screen: the changed card is drawn back to the bench edge and the card it replaced returns to its tray, and both trays are then worked on the cards they share. The product the changed card would have given is worked in a third small row beneath the ledge and stood beside the other two, where it does not match either of them.

phases.screen: the same cards in both trays, arranged differently in each
phases.soWhat: Swapping the two numbers, or bracketing a different pair, leaves the product alone, so pick the arrangement you would rather work.
phases.concept: The order is yours to choose

phases.win: the parts add to the same product the whole number gave, standing beside it
phases.does: multiplies each part in its own row, then adds the rows up
phases.goal: a multiplicand split by place gives parts that multiply separately and add back
phases.says: Break it into its places. Multiply each piece. Now put the pieces back together.
phases.check: Which of these is another way to find 65 x 7: (60 x 7) + (5 x 7), or (60 + 7) x (5 + 7)?
phases.feels: the pieces are small enough to do in the head, and they still add back to the whole thing
phases.hands: Write 625 on paper as 600 + 20 + 5, multiply each part by 5 in its own line, and add the three lines up. Then work 625 x 5 in columns beside it. Ask which of the two they could have done without writing anything down at all.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what are the places of the number being broken up? Second rung, the phase's: what has to happen to every one of those parts? Third rung: the strip is cut to a two digit number split into its tens and its ones, and the child works both small rows and adds them. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the hundreds part is worth far more than the other two put together, and an answer that is nearly right feels like an answer that is finished.
wrong.move: multiplies the hundreds part, stops there, and reads that as the answer.
wrong.screen: the two parts that were never taken stay on the strip drawn grey with their small rows left empty and ringed, and the total the child gave is stood against the total of all three rows, with the gap between them written out beside it as the two parts that were left behind: 3000 given, 3125 wanted, and 100 and 25 never taken.

wrong.why: once the multiplicand has been split, splitting the other number looks like the same move made twice, and two rows of parts standing level with each other invite being read straight across.
wrong.move: breaks the multiplier into parts as well, pairs each part off with the part standing level with it, and adds just those products.
wrong.screen: a line is drawn from every part of the one number to every part of the other, so the pairings the child never made show up as lines with nothing written on them; the strip then closes the multiplier back into a single card and each part of the multiplicand is taken by the whole of it in turn. The child's rows stay on the bench while both readings are worked.

phases.screen: the expand and add strip with the multiplicand broken into its hundreds, tens and ones
phases.soWhat: Break the multiplicand into its places, multiply every one of those places, and add the parts.
phases.concept: A number can be broken up before it is multiplied

phases.win: the digits stay put, the zeros open beneath them and the rail names the places they fill
phases.does: multiplies by ten, then by a hundred, then by a multiple, counting the zeros each time
phases.goal: a round multiplier is handled by a short fact and the zeros it carries
phases.says: Say how many zeros will follow before you press. Then press and count them.
phases.check: 58 x 7 = 406. What is 58 x 7000, and how many zeros did the multiplier carry?
phases.feels: the digits stay exactly as they were and the only thing that changes is how many places have opened under them
phases.hands: On paper write 398 x 6, and under it write 398 x 60. Work the first, then look hard at the second before working it. Do the same with 234 x 8 and 234 x 800. Each time, say out loud how many zeros will follow before a single one is written.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many zeros are printed in the multiplier? Second rung, the phase's: where do those zeros go once the short fact has been worked? Third rung: the rail is cut to a two digit number multiplied by ten, and the child opens that single place by hand. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the short fact is the piece that has just been worked, so its digits are the ones under the eye, and a zero already in the answer looks like a zero that has been accounted for.
wrong.move: counts the zeros already sitting in the short fact and writes those, instead of the zeros the multiplier carries.
wrong.screen: the multiplier is drawn on its own above the rail with its zeros ringed and counted out loud, and then that many empty places open under the right hand end of the short fact one at a time, each naming itself as it opens. The child's answer stands beside the rail with the places it is short of left open and ringed, and neither number is cleared.

wrong.why: a number grows at its left hand end when it is written out, so the room that opens up for a bigger answer looks as though it belongs at the front of it.
wrong.move: opens the new places in front of the number instead of after it, so the zeros land at the leading end.
wrong.screen: the number is read out place by place with the zeros where the child put them, and then again with them at the other end, and the two readings are written one under the other along the rail with the place names lit under every digit of both. The leading zeros are heard naming nothing at all, and the child's reading is left standing.

phases.screen: the zeros rail with the number above it and empty places opening to its right
phases.soWhat: Use the short fact first, then write as many zeros as the multiplier carries.
phases.concept: Zeros at the end do the work for you

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the first time a number is sent along the zeros rail. The digits do not jump and nothing is redrawn. One empty place opens under the right hand end of the number and the whole number slides one place to the left into it, with the place names lighting under each digit as they pass, ones becoming tens, tens becoming hundreds, all the way along. Ask for a hundred and two places open and the same slide happens twice over. Send the number back and the places close one at a time and the digits walk home. The same cards are worth hundreds in one position and hundreds of thousands three positions along, and not one of them was ever rewritten.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase one long number lies in the left tray with a one card and a zero card waiting on the corner of the bench beside it. On the second the same cards lie in both trays in two different arrangements and neither tray has been worked. On the third the expand and add strip stands open under the trays with a three digit multiplicand already broken into its hundreds, tens and ones and every small row beneath it empty. On the fourth the zeros rail runs along the foot of the bench with a number sitting above it and the places to its right still closed. The running count at the top left holds the arrangements worked against the arrangements standing on the bench, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the one card, or the right hand tray, or the first broken part, or the first closed place on the rail, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the bench is going to do. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any cards in either tray, brackets anywhere, with the expand strip, the zeros rail and the pairing bay open alongside. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on multiplying by one and by zero, choosing the order, expanding a multiplicand and using the zeros of a round multiplier.
voiceLines: The same cards in both trays, arranged two different ways. Work them both.
Take the number once. Now take it no times at all. What came back each time?
Swap them over, then work both trays. Did the product move?
Break it into its places. Multiply each piece. Now put the pieces back together.
Say how many zeros will follow before you press. Then press and count them.
New cards on the bench. Choose the arrangement you would rather work.
Free play. Any cards, brackets anywhere, with the expand strip and the zeros rail open.
Put the cards back and let the trays work the two arrangements side by side.
You changed the arrangement every single time, and the product never moved.

observations.why: Changing the arrangement changes which multiplication is done first and how many rows it takes, and it leaves the answer exactly where it was.
observations.soWhat: The product is what a swap promises. The steps are not, so choose the arrangement you would rather write out.
observations.observe: Both trays landed on the same product, and the working drawn under the two of them did not look the same.

observations.why: Taking a number once is the number itself, and taking it no times at all is nothing, however many digits it had.
observations.soWhat: Neither of those two multipliers needs any working at all.
observations.observe: The one card handed the number straight back and the zero card emptied the tray, whatever length of number was in it.

observations.why: The hundreds, the tens and the ones are the number itself written apart, so taking each of them five times takes the whole number five times.
observations.soWhat: Breaking a multiplicand up before multiplying is allowed, and it makes every step small enough to hold in the head.
observations.observe: The parts of 625 broken up and multiplied came to 3000 and 100 and 25, and those add back to the same 3125 the whole number gave.

observations.why: Multiplying by ten, a hundred or a thousand moves every digit one, two or three places to the left, and the places left behind have to be held open by zeros.
observations.soWhat: Count the zeros the multiplier carries, not the zeros that happen to be sitting in the short fact you used.
observations.observe: On the rail the digits never changed. The only thing that changed was how many places had opened underneath them.

phases.screen: a tray holding one long number, with a one card and a zero card waiting beside it
phases.win: the first tray hands the number back unchanged and the second collapses to nothing
phases.traceback: The cards drop again, slowly: the one card sends one group of the number down to the ledge, the zero card sends no group and the tray empties, and each product is written out in full.
ladder: How many times does the zero card take the number?
The one card takes the number just once. What comes back?
The zero card asks for zero groups of the number. What does the ledge hold then?
What is left when a number is taken no times at all?
Think of 12 × 1 and 12 × 0 first. Then do the same with this number.

phases.screen: the same cards in both trays, arranged differently in each
phases.win: both trays land on the same product and the pairing bay lights the pair that makes a round number
phases.traceback: Both trays are worked on their own arrangements, slowly, every step drawn: the long number on the mat in one row with its carries, the short one on the mat in a row per place (or each grouping in two lines); the two products land side by side and match.
ladder: Put 427 on top. When 7 × 6 makes 42, where do the 4 tens go?
With 312 on top, 2 × 8 makes 16. Which column does its 1 ten go to?
Which two cards make a round number? Count the zeros it brings.
What does changing their order do to the product?
Pick the arrangement that is easiest to work. Then multiply it one step at a time.

phases.screen: the expand and add strip with the multiplicand broken into its hundreds, tens and ones
phases.win: the parts add to the same product the whole number gave, standing beside it
phases.traceback: The parts never taken are ringed, then the multiplier takes each of them in turn; the rows add to the total, and the whole number worked in its own column lands on the same product beside it.
ladder: Did the 300, the 40 and the 8 each get a row in the total?
Add all three rows. Did the 20 and the 6 go into your total too?
Does that way take the 8 as well as the 40?
What has to happen to every one of those parts?
Take every part with the whole multiplier. Then add all the rows together.

phases.screen: the zeros rail with the number above it and empty places opening to its right
phases.win: the digits stay put, the zeros open beneath them and the rail names the places they fill
phases.traceback: The zeros of the numbers are ringed and counted one at a time, the short fact is worked above the rail, and then that many places open under its right hand end one at a time, each naming itself.
ladder: How many zeros are printed in 4,000?
What is 264 × 7? Then how many zeros does 700 carry?
Count the zeros in 20 and in 300 together.
Where do those zeros go once the short fact has been worked?
Work the short fact first. Then count the zeros the multiplier carries.

colours.carry: vermilion, small, in a ring above its column

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The cards drop again, slowly: the one card sends one group of the number down to the ledge, the zero card sends no group and the tray empties, and each product is written out in full.

Phase 2: Both trays are worked on their own arrangements, slowly, every step drawn: the long number on the mat in one row with its carries, the short one on the mat in a row per place (or each grouping in two lines); the two products land side by side and match.

Phase 3: The parts never taken are ringed, then the multiplier takes each of them in turn; the rows add to the total, and the whole number worked in its own column lands on the same product beside it.

Phase 4: The zeros of the numbers are ringed and counted one at a time, the short fact is worked above the rail, and then that many places open under its right hand end one at a time, each naming itself.

voice.opening: The same cards in both trays, arranged two different ways. Work them both.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: You changed the arrangement every single time, and the product never moved.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planQuestion: What is 4826 x 1, and what is 4826 x 0?

question.en: What is 4,826 × 1? And what is 4,826 × 0? Pick your answer, then drop each card into a tray.
What is 5,307 × 1? Type it, then drop the card into the tray.
What is 6,941 × 0? Type it first, then let the zero card fall in.

items.planQuestion: Find 6 x 427 by changing the order of the two numbers.

question.en: Find 6 × 427 by changing the order of the two numbers. Tap a card to swap them.

items.planQuestion: Find 8 x 312 by putting the longer number on the mat first.

question.en: Find 8 × 312 by putting the longer number on the mat first.

items.planQuestion: Find 372 x 5 x 20 by pairing two of the numbers first.

question.en: Find 372 × 5 × 20 by pairing two of the numbers first. Tap a sign to bracket a pair, then type what it makes.

items.planAnswer: 37,200, by multiplying 5 and 20 first to make 100

items.planQuestion: Expand the multiplicand and find 348 x 6.

question.en: Expand the multiplicand and find 348 × 6. Drop the 6 card on a part, then type what that part makes.

items.planQuestion: Expand the multiplicand and find 526 x 4.

question.en: Find 526 × 4 the same way, one part at a time.

items.planQuestion: Which of these is another way to find 48 x 9: (40 x 9) + (8 x 9), or (40 + 9) x (8 + 9)?

question.en: Which is another way to find 48 × 9? Tap the 48 to break it, then pick on the pad.

items.planAnswer: (40 x 9) + (8 x 9), because it comes to 360 + 72 = 432, which is what 48 x 9 comes to

items.planQuestion: Find 473 x 10, then 473 x 100, then 473 x 4000.

question.en: Now find 473 × 4,000. Type it, then drop the card on the rail.
Find 264 × 700. Type the product first, then send the card along.

items.planAnswer: 1,84,800, because 264 x 7 = 1848 and the multiplier carries two zeros

items.planQuestion: A strip holds 20 tablets and a carton holds 300 such strips. How many tablets are in the carton?

question.en: A strip holds 20 tablets and a carton holds 300 such strips. How many tablets are in the carton?

items.planAnswer: 6000 tablets, because 2 x 3 = 6 and the two numbers carry three zeros between them

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy

scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once.
